business.offer: A 12-week one-on-one rehab and strength program for runners, delivered in-clinic in Austin with weekly check-ins
business.price_point: $2,400 per program, paid up front or in three installments
business.buyer: The runner themselves — no insurance, no referrals, they find the clinic on Instagram and book a free 20-minute assessment
business.note: Viewer and buyer are the same person, so content can speak straight to the runner.

avatar.name: Comeback Chris
avatar.portrait: A 38-year-old marketing manager who ran his first marathon at 33, got hooked, and has been fighting a knee that flares up past mile 10 for the last eighteen months. He has a Garmin, a foam roller he ignores, and a race registration he is scared he will have to defer again.
believes: Rest is the only real fix
PTs just hand you a sheet of clamshells
fears: Being told to stop running for good
Wasting another $150 on a session that changes nothing
Deferring the race a second time
complains_about: I did the exercises and it still hurts
Every answer online contradicts the last one

dream_outcome: Cross the finish line of his next marathon pain-free, and know he can keep running into his 50s.

pain_points.text: Why does my knee only hurt after mile 10?
Do I actually have to stop running to heal?
Why did two rounds of PT not fix this?
Should I run through pain or rest until it's gone?
Is it my shoes, my form, or my hips?
How much strength work does a runner really need?
Can I still hit my goal time after an injury?
What should a return-to-running week look like?

authority_statement.recommended: I help injured marathoners get back to pain-free running without giving up the race.
alternates: I help runners in their 30s and 40s with knee and hip injuries that keep coming back.
authority_statement.why: It names the person (injured marathoners), the outcome (pain-free running), and the fear it removes (giving up the race). The alternates are either narrower on the injury or too short to carry the outcome.

attributes.name: Topic
attributes.evidence: Return-to-running for injured marathoners is far narrower than the generic 'runner's knee' content that dominates the space.

attributes.name: Substance
attributes.evidence: Twelve years treating runners plus her own two marathon comebacks; she can show gait video, not just exercises.

attributes.name: Avatar
attributes.evidence: One person, one situation: the 30s-40s marathoner scared of deferring again.

attributes.name: Format
attributes.evidence: Filming real gait assessments with patients is unusual, but she hasn't tested it on camera yet.

attributes.name: Visuals
attributes.evidence: Standard clinic setting, nothing distinctive yet on screen.

hypothesis.lane: The lane is 'the physio who watches you run.' Most competitors post exercise lists filmed in a gym; Maya can post real gait breakdowns of real comeback runners, tied to a single promise: back to the start line, pain-free. That is a topic, substance, and avatar lane, and the format may become the visual signature if the gait footage lands.

one_thing: When someone needs to get back to running after an injury, I want to be the first name they think of.
filter_questions: Would this be worth Comeback Chris's time?
Would it make him trust me more?
